So I would normally write a review trying to be funny but instead I'll tell you why this game is so awesome instead.

Starting off, the pacing. This game is not like other FPS games. No matter your playstyle, you must adapt when you play Ready or Not. Running and gunning will get you nowhere because 1-3 shots is all it takes to kill. This does not exclude you. You are not a superhero like Superman or Ironman who can take shots and scoff them off. There are other games like this, examples being CSGO or Hotline Miami, but what separates them from this game is that death genuinely matters. You are a swat officer, a human being in a setting where life is fragile and fleeting. If you decide to run around a corner before checking for hostiles or if you slam open a door you run the risk of being shot in the head and dying on the spot or having yourself blown to smithereens by door traps. This would be cool and all, but death could mean restarting the entire mission or getting an evac. The developers literally did not implement a sprint option in the game just to reinforce that you do not rush this game. You must play very slow and steady, meticulously checking off an invisible list of safety precautions around every corner. And on top of this, if you end up dying the game likes to send you back to the police station where you end up going through what feels like 7 different intermissions just to replay the mission.

Next great thing, the environmental storytelling. The game does not directly tell you the story of the game. If you stripped the game of all textures and left everything else the same you would miss out on 60% of the experience. Going through the aftermath of where horrible tragedy took place and just looking around, learning the story of what took place in the building you are raiding is such a really well executed part of the game. For instance, in the mission where you try to take control of a gas station robbery, there is a ringing phone on the floor next to the manager's mangled body that will never be answered. In The Spider, there are posters on the walls of Brixley Talent Time that show the faces of the child victims who were traded into Brixley's hands. In Twisted Nerve, there is a child's bedroom in the crackhouse that shows one of the victims who is an innocent little girl, dying in her bed as a music box plays in the background. These are just my favorite examples. There are hundreds more I could list but it would take all day.

Lastly, the freedom. In Ready or Not, you have the freedom to choose any combination of weapons or attachments, tools, field equipment, ect. as it is all available to you from the second you step foot in the police station. If you don't want to hurt anyone, there's a playstyle and loadout you can make for that. If you want to go 'no russian', there is a loadout you can make for that. If you want to go in with nothing at all, I am like 90% sure you can do that too. And then the freedom for missions as well, if you join a public lobby all the missions are unlocked for you to play with friends. Also you can do friendly fire and grief your whole squad if you want lol

Before I started playing this game, there was quite the divide between my wife and I. She wasn't a big fan of video games, but I spend a decent amount of time playing them. I always tried to get her to play with me, but she always refused. She'd say, "It's just not fun for me. I'm not good."

But then I downloaded "Ready or Not," and everything immediately changed.

The gameplay is smooth, and the graphics are much better than I expected. The gun mechanics are the most realistic I've ever seen in a game. There is a surprising variety in types of enemies and civilians. It's always a rush when you have to make a split second decision on whether you're about to shoot a person in defense, or take an innocent civilian's life. It has been a long time since I enjoyed a game this much.

I am a sucker for milsim games. I've played anything from DCS, Operation Flashpoint, Arma, Hell Let Loose, etc. so when I saw a SWAT game that looked pretty realistic, and from the many clips I saw on social media, I just had to give it a try.

Since most combat simulations revolve around the military, seeing a law enforcement game pull that level of realism immediately had my attention. Now, don't take it from me, I cannot speak on if it's truly 1:1 with reality. I've never served in the military or law enforcement to any capacity, but this game really immerses you. Looking back to relatively recent history all the way back to 50 years ago, this game definitely shares elements of the worst case scenarios and most intense law enforcement clashes in history. So basing it off historical events, this game comes pretty close.

As for immersion in-game, as a well traveled simulation player, this game has it all. For starters, the customization of pretty much everything is amazing. You can't customize character's body features outside of tattoos which is nice. I hate spending 20+ minutes designing characters only to look like an ogre. But you can customize your kit from the weapons you carry, what's on those weapons, the ammo type, grenades, armor type and coverage if any task oriented gear like shields, mirrors, and, well, you get the picture. But not only can you do this for your character, in single-player, you go in with a squad of 5 (including yourself) and you can customize just as much with your squad as you do yourself to suit the mission with the ability to save loadouts so you don't have to spend 30 minutes in pre-mission decking your team out. The AI all around is also insane. Your team will issue orders to civilians and suspects, will detain everyone they come across and bag evidence along the way with or without orders if it's safe enough to do so. The civilians will do dumb things that may make it seem like they're a threat when it's just a phone they're reaching for. "Dead" suspects may not be so dead. I played a mission where I shot a guy and he collapsed but I pushed passed him to clear the connecting room so I wouldn't get shot trying to arrest someone and the "dead" guy was just faking it. He waited until I stepped over him, stood up, and stabbed in the back. They'll also flee if they can and run circles around you until you run into each other again.

Speaking of single-player, not only do you deploy with a squad, you are given a command tab that allows you to control your team any way you see fit. Want to breach a door? Go right ahead, but HOW is the question. Want breaching charges? Maybe a shotgun to blow the lock? Maybe simplicity is bliss and you just want to kick the door in, flash and clear. Those are just a few examples with several more options available depending on how you kitted your team. For the most part, your AI teammates are competent and watch your back, follow your commands to a tee, and will even continue clearing buildings if no further commands are given. Some of the best, non-scripted friendly AI I've ever seen in a game. I've only had a few instances where they didn't do what they were supposed to do which I feel has something to do with their stress levels... yes, as team leader, you have to choose who you take on missions and manage stress levels... it is THAT in-depth.

As for multiplayer, you lose your AI squad but that's kind of the point. You NEED to work as a team with your friends if you want to survive, let alone win. It's all the same missions but with the added difficulty of usually fewer numbers and human error. Generally, the AI doesn't mistake civilians for threats and visa versa.

Controls... ah yes, what most new simulation players fear. I am happy to say this is the least complicated sim game I've ever come across. You have a key for quick commands and a key for the command menu. Weapons are universally the same as far as aim and shoot, however you have a key for attachments (one for zoom if applicable and one for light/laser if applicable). You have two different aiming methods which you can switch between whenever: sights and canted. You have hot keys for grenades and the previously mentioned quick command which will change depending on what you're looking at. Movement is universally the same, WASD+QE, a key for crouch, and a key for, what I call "free-lean," where you can crouch low to check underneath various objects and peer around corners with a little bit more flexibility. The rest of your gear is, by default, your numbers. Any item box with an arrow means you can use your wheel to select exactly what you want if multiple items are under the same category (ie. grenades, less lethal, etc.). Best part, the keybindings are customizable to suit every player.

Story. Well, it's complicated. There technically is a story however it's not as linear and black and white as, say, Call of Duty. There are missions that are connected to each other via evidence you come across and underlying clues to bigger elements. But like the daily life as law enforcement, each mission is different and not every case is connected.

Character development... non existent. In fact, there are only a few parts where anyone shows any form of emotion. Otherwise, all eyes are forward and all anyone is worried about is completing the mission.

Themes... well this is the most sensitive part. I'm a rational person and usually don't get mad at elements of a video game... however... there are some pretty rage inducing parts of the game simply because of the fact a lot of this has happened under similar circumstances. This is obviously not a game for kids, but there are some adults that may find this game VERY disturbing, or even upsetting. However, no matter what you come across and see, just know, the developers did an amazing job at not glorifying or encouraging anything. The game is very dark and parts were clearly meant to invoke an angry response to emphasize the tragedies and how horrific and close to home some of it is.

DLC and future updates. My favorite part and, what I'd assume, many more are concerned with. The devs are continuously working to improve and add to the game. As of this post, they recently just released their new Dark Waters DLC with new missions and weapons. The DLC is just as action packed as the main game but with even less story than there already was. Still fun nonetheless. From what I can tell though, the weapons are part of the updates which is free. The only extras you're paying for is missions. Great flexibility for players who want new gear but don't want to pay a large price for more content than they're looking for.

Cons... My least favorite part. For starters, you don't have a save feature. This game runs on auto save which only happens when you change your kit or upon completion of a mission. If you leave mid mission, it negatively impacts the morale of your squad and may cause them to quit as well as you having to restart that mission from the beginning. Any special perks they had are then gone and you'll have to hire replacements which may or may not have the same perks. It's just a luck of the draw. The missions can be rather long too depending on how meticulous and methodical you choose to be. The longest mission took me about 15 minutes to complete just running and gunning. Playing it methodically took me about an hour. Each mission is vastly different with maps being all sizes which will greatly vary mission time. To me this isn't an issue, but this is not a game I'd play if I'm on a time crunch. Lastly, no game is perfect. This game does occasionally bug out a little.

If you've made it this far, this game is obviously spiked your interest and I greatly appreciate your time. It may be a long review but there are too many games where it's just people praising or complaining about the game and not giving people a chance to understand what they're buying.

Ready or Not is a tactical shooter game in the style of Sierra's former SWAT 3 & 4 games.

You can select all of your equipment before a mission, including many details regarding its appearance. However, new equipment is only unlocked after successfully completing missions at a certain rank.

The missions can be difficult at first, but you'll remember the difficult points by repeating them. To get to grips with all the details of a mission, it's recommended to play it in single-player first, where you can also plan the entire tactical approach of the task force.

Overall, it's SWAT 5, even if the mission presentation could have been a bit more atmospheric, with short intro videos, for example, but it's still a definite recommendation.

This is an extremely painful review for me to make.
The game itself is great; a more grounded shooter where your main goal is to defuse situations and only kill if out of options. An extremely immersive experience with a selection of guns and tools to pick from. Due to how heated the situations can get and how fragile you are, it can give you a surprising rush.

Unfortunately, to say that the most recent direction the game has taken has been extremely poorly received would be an understatement. Los Sueños Stories, dubbed the "console update" by the playerbase, has seen a long list of negative changes to the game: a graphical downgrade, many of bugs that have yet to be squashed, and several changes meant to censor the game for the console release that, for some unholy reason, have also been included in the PC version. Less gore and nudity is already stupid enough as is, but it does include changing the girl in Twisted Nerve from convulsing due to drug overdose to just sleeping all soundly unaware of the gunshots taking place, and to change the eponymous basement room in Valley of the Dolls, replacing pictures of the main suspect's daughter with just plastic dolls. These changes lessen the impact of these moments, and in the latter case are extra stupid because the plastic doll change is only there in the console versions - if the devs can make separate changes for both console and PC, then why censor the PC to begin with?! I cannot wrap my head around this - Valley of the Dolls room clearly shows that they [i]can[/i] do it, they just decided not to.

The other problem is, with the console update, [b]all of mod.io was basically wiped[/b]. While it is true that a lot of past mods have been crashing the game on the newest version, with the state the community is in, vast majority of these mods have not been updated. Over a month since the update, and the mod page is still mostly barren. This especially annoys me because before the update I have seen several levels ported over from SWAT 4, the game's spiritual predecessor, and I was actually pissed off when I realised they're all gone now, and not likely to be restored to working order. There is a grand total of [i]three[/i] custom levels available on mod.io as of writing.

[i]Ready or Not[/i] is... [i]was[/i] a great game, that unfortunately was destroyed by its devs when they tried to appeal to console manufacturers, then later abandoned by the community with most of its modding scene stripped out. As much as I want to recommend it, I cannot due to all the circumstances around it.

To the developers of Ready or Not,

We, your dedicated player base, write this with heavy hearts and a profound sense of disappointment. Ready or Not was once a beacon in the tactical shooter genre, a game that not only challenged us with its demanding gameplay but also resonated with its unflinching portrayal of the moral complexities faced by SWAT officers. It captured the gritty realism and difficult choices reminiscent of classics like SWAT 4, pushing players to confront uncomfortable truths and make split-second decisions with significant consequences. We invested our time, our passion, and our money into this vision, completing achievements, introducing friends, and eagerly anticipating its evolution.

However, recent updates have systematically dismantled the very foundations of what made Ready or Not exceptional. The drive for console ESRB approval has led to the censorship of key story content, stripping away narrative impact and altering the game's intended tone. The "Valley of the Dolls" map, once a masterclass in atmosphere and moral strain, has been rendered a shadow of its former self, and crucial narrative moments, like the altered "girl in the spider" scenario, now fall flat, robbed of their original visceral power.

Equally devastating is the significant downgrade in graphical fidelity. We are now grappling with broken lighting systems, marred by jarring checkerboard artifacts, and noticeably degraded textures that reduce legibility and overall visual quality. The persistent issue of LOD pop-in, always a concern, has been exacerbated to unacceptable levels, even on maximum settings, with world models visibly degrading just feet away. This visual regression feels like a betrayal of the PC experience we were promised.

We feel as though we have paid for a superior PC experience, only to have it compromised and delivered as a lesser console port. This is not a minor setback; it is a fundamental degradation of the game we loved. We implore you, VOID, to acknowledge the depth of this disappointment. We urge you to consider reverting the detrimental changes, particularly to the AI and graphics, or to provide transparency regarding the specific constraints you are facing. Our hope is that you will address these issues with the urgency they deserve, restoring Ready or Not to its former glory and respecting the investment and passion of your player base.

Since the console update dropped, figured I’d circle back and update this review.

Rig used for this revisit: 7800X3D, 4090 OC, 64GB RAM, NVMe, Windows 11 24Hxx.

Basically, on top of key story content getting censored, just so the game could get ESRB approval for a console disc release, they’ve quietly downgraded the PC version’s graphics.

Lighting is partially broken now, some of it is prebaked, but the quality is poor, and in certain spots you’ll see this weird checkerboard style grid surrounding the baked lighting. It sticks out bad.

Textures have taken a hit, some things are noticeably less legible, resolution has been clipped in spots, and overall texture quality feels softer than before.

A few world models had their LODs retooled, but not for the better. RoN has always suffered from LOD pop in, even on epic settings, native 4K, with DLAA, but it’s worse now. Specifically in Neon Tomb’s lower basement bathrooms, near the “peeing” neon signs, you can stand right in front of the hand dryers and watch them pop into a low detail model just a few feet away. That’s unacceptable with everything maxed out.

I’ve also run into multiple instances where civilians are bugged out and flat out refuse to surrender, beanbags, pepperballs, flashes, stingers, nothing works. They stand there locked in some dead animation. This was never an issue before the console update, not like this.

So on top of new bugs, we’ve lost graphical fidelity, got the storyline censored, and the overall experience has just gotten worse compared to 1.0.

Honestly, it’s disappointing, feels like we all paid for the proper PC experience, and now we’re stuck playing a console version instead.

If you bought this game in or after September 2025: I'm sorry, you were too late, and you got the raw end of the deal. The best time to play this game was between Christmas of 2023 and August of 2025, between the 1.0 launch and the console update, where its soul was gutted and sacrificed on the altar of appealing to the puritanist megacorporations of Sony and Microsoft. What remains is a dementia patient. A decrepit husk, ostensibly the same person on the surface, but the soul walked out long ago, never to return.

During this "golden age" (and even before in many aspects), this game was sublime. It dared to not pull any of the punches it set out to strike. It brutally realistically depicted real-world events and made you feel bad even if you got the "good outcome", and there's some considerable debate on whether some of these scenarios even had a good outcome, or what it was. The game was difficult to run with high FPS, not because of lacking optimisation (or at least not just that...), but because the maps were packed so chock full of detail and lore that some YouTubers made a living out of oogling over single pieces of paper on desks and emails left on screens and speculating what they might mean to the story.

In short, this game made you [i]feel[/i]. It made you feel a lot of things: Sad, outraged, angered, disgusted, sometimes physically ill. But it also made you feel begrudgingly proud, relieved, sometimes faintly hopeful. All in all, it often made you feel conflicted. It was a game that dared to be subtle, to not obnoxiously highlight the connecting aspects of the story in quotation marks and red text, and it had the confidence to leave it up to the players to discover the dotted line of the larger story running through the standard gameplay of the individual missions.

In contrast, the game past the console update is in some aspects still the same, but its soul has been surgically removed only so that the puritanism boards of Sony and Microsoft would graciously allow this masterpiece into their pretentious walled gardens. It has gone towards being Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2019 in terms of storytelling; pretending to throw punches, but then obscuring the main event with a cloud of smoke to avoid a higher age rating. It has gone from just showing the player the horrific scene to implying its existence. "Tell, don't show". Apart from the bits where some of the missions have been crudely retconned to just deny the existence of the horrific scene altogether. Some of the biggest reveals in the entire game that used to make your jaw hit the floor and that were so emblematic of the "VOID Interactive gut punch" at the end of a level have been crudely censored to a point where they don't even make factual sense anymore. The level of detail has also come down several orders of magnitude to run properly on tacky oversized calculators in TV stands, so now the game just runs like shit full stop instead of running like shit because the level of detail was so high.

So, if you're here in 2026 and wondering whether you should buy this, I'm sorry to tell you that you're late. The game that people talked about in 2024 and 2025 isn't this one. It's one you can't get anymore. It's not even the game shown in some of the trailers and screenshots, because those are from before the game was gutted on the altar of consoles, making it tantamount to false advertising.

If you think Modern Warfare 2019's Clean House multiplied into two dozen levels is still worth your money, go ahead. But I'm here to tell you this game used to be so much more than that in times past, and you missed out. And that's a damn shame.

(P.S: I know the uncensor mod exists. It doesn't put all of it back. And Lord knows how long it'll continue functioning.)

Ready or Not is a game I really want to recommend, but in its current state I can’t.

The core of the game is genuinely great. The maps are well designed, the atmosphere is fantastic, and the game offers a really satisfying variety of weapons, attachments, and tactical equipment. The DLCs are also solid and add some great locations and scenarios. When everything works, it can be one of the most immersive tactical shooters out there.

Unfortunately the AI completely ruins the experience.

Suspects often feel like you're playing against aimbotters rather than human enemies. Even on standard difficulty they react instantly, track you through impossible angles, and land near perfect shots the moment you expose a pixel. Instead of encouraging careful tactical play, it frequently turns encounters into frustrating coin flips. On top of that suspects can often shoot through walls and pillars, sometimes even with pistols, which makes using cover feel unreliable or completely pointless at times.

Another major issue is that NPC models do not always sync with their actions. You can use the Mirrorgun under a door and clearly see a suspect facing away from it, yet the moment the door opens they react instantly as if they were already watching it. Suspects can also shoot you while not even looking in your direction. These kinds of desyncs completely break the tactical aspect of the game because the visual information you rely on is not trustworthy.

Civilians are also strangely implemented and frequently break immersion. In situations where they are supposed to be hostages in an active police operation, many of them behave with a bizarre level of attitude toward the officers trying to rescue them. They talk trash to the police, run around unpredictably, and sometimes even move straight into the middle of suspects. Instead of feeling like frightened people in a dangerous situation, they often behave as if they don’t grasp the seriousness of what’s happening.

The achievements make this even worse. Many of them are either bugged or borderline impossible because of the AI behavior. Trying to complete them stops being a challenge and becomes pure frustration.

What makes this more disappointing is that it often feels like the developers don’t actually play their own game. If they did, it’s hard to imagine these AI behaviors and achievement requirements making it into the live version in their current state.

There’s an amazing tactical shooter buried here with great maps, great equipment, and great atmosphere, but until the AI is seriously reworked, civilians behave more realistically, and achievements are fixed, the experience feels more frustrating than rewarding.
Good game, but the devs are shameless pathetic sellouts who abandoned their core fan base for money.

With this game's 1.0 release, I feel like it's time to voice my deep concerns regarding this game's development and future status. This will be a review that doesn't restate anything you can read in the game's Steam description, and will instead focus on my thoughts about the game after 220 hours of play according to Steam at time of writing.

[h2] Performance Issues and Bugs[/h2]

Consistently, ever since I first purchased this game, up to the present 1.0 release, I have experienced performance issues with the game, even at the lowest settings. This is not a feature of My Machine™ alone, but a common experience I've seen between my fellow players and I. 

 - Framerates will regularly tank when entering or viewing large areas with many assets.
 - Stuttering when turning the camera around the room.
 - A feature of this latest update are seconds-long freeze frames in the middle of combat, which predictably lead to the death of the player.

Ready or Not is victim to numerous bugs, many of which are centered around the game's poorly implemented physics engine. For instance, pieces of evidence dropped by suspects will often phase several feet into the floor, which is now well revealed by the accessibility feature to highlight dropped evidence(a good recent addition). No doubt some of the performance issues can be classified as game-breaking bugs, like the screen-freezes.

[h2] Suspect Design [/h2]

This being a police game, the suspects are *the* primary source of gameplay. Without suspects, there is no need for a SWAT team, no need to yell or shoot at anyone. Thus, it's fairly obvious that the suspects in this game need to be well balanced for an enjoyable experience. While VOID has put a lot of effort into the creation of the suspects in this game, there are a number of issues that need to be addressed.

 - Suspects are extremely accurate, and will often hit players with fatal gunfire within one or two seconds of entering their line of sight.
 - Suspects are extremely decisive, and will usually initiate a fight with the SWAT team, even if they have not been fired at first.
 - Suspects are extremely hardy, and will continue to fight even after receiving multiple gunshot wounds. Somehow, they appear to surrender more quickly after being struck with beanbags than with real bullets.

Notice the use of *'extremely'* in the previous three points, and I think it's a good summary to describe RoN's suspects as *extreme.* They do not represent what one could reasonably expect even from trained and committed foes. They will fight like soldiers. Ironically, I would petition VOID Interactive to take cues from the AI of a game focused entirely on enemy soldiers: F.E.A.R.

While the AI in F.E.A.R. are representing a different kind of foe than usually faced in RoN, somehow they appear to behave as better foes than RoN's suspects. When encountering the player, they will often take cover rather than immediately engage, they are *rarely* perfectly accurate, they will often be stunned for 5 or even 10 seconds when shot, they interact with their environments more, in an attempt to gain an advantage over the player.

I don't advise copying and pasting F.E.A.R.'s replica soldiers into RoN, but taking cues from their design would do a lot of good I feel. Replica soldiers on the extreme difficulty of the game can be said to almost be the player's equal in ability. The suspects in RoN do not feel like equals, but like robots who can occasionally be convinced to surrender. This is the core gameplay of a tactical police shooter, so a failure to design good suspects is a failure to design a good game.

[h2] Scenario Design [/h2]

Every scenario which the team enters has to be designed to fit the concept. For instance, a group of violent youths holding up a Gas Station for drug money is a scenario, so you shouldn't expect to face a professional army once you enter the premises. One would also hope that the scenarios depicted in a realistic police game are ones which maintain the player's immersion in the story, without introducing absurd elements like space elves. RoN fails on both of these grounds.

 - Scenarios will often have suspects whose abilities, behaviour and morale do not match what could be reasonably expected of the description. A gang of youths robbing a gas station for money should not behave like hardened terrorists willing to die for $200.
 - Scenarios will often feature an excessive number of suspects. The best example of this is the Streamer map, which features a veritable army of suspects for what should be warrant service against a *single* murderer. Apparently, it seems there's an entirely unrelated *gang* in this apartment building. Why couldn't VOID Interactive be satisfied with this being a level that has a single suspect, or maybe two?
- Because of these facts, and the game's habit of turning every scenario up to 11, and linking them together with shared features, the game damages the player's immersion. Maybe we're not literally fighting space elves, but sometimes it does feel like the Eldar have landed an army and disguised themselves as corporate security or disgrunted military veterans.

[h2] In the Shadow of SWAT 4[/h2]

For those who aren't in the know, SWAT 4 is a nearly 20 year old tactical shooter oriented around a SWAT team performing high risk warrant services and counter-terror operations in a fictional American city. Ready or Not has been lauded as a spiritual successor to SWAT 4. Having played and enjoyed SWAT 4, I have to notice that RoN has failed to inherit the best features of SWAT 4.

 - Consistent and Bug-Free Performance: While I don't have the benefit of knowing what SWAT 4 performed like at release, I can say for certain that it runs perfectly well on my machine today and I haven't encountered or noticed any game breaking bugs, stuttering or freezes. This should be considered a bare minimum for a video game which is no longer a "beta".
- Difficult but Fair Suspects: Suspects in SWAT 4 can often be deadly accurate like RoN's suspects, but rarely do they initiate a fight within the first few seconds of spotting the SWAT team. Often, they will retreat to cover, or hesitate, which is a realistic response to the arrival of a tactical team, even for some of the game's more deadly foes, like trained terrorists.
- Sane Scenario Design: SWAT 4's scenarios are often unusual, featuring warrant service against cults, gun smugglers, terrorists and even foreign intelligence agents. But they are fitting for a *special* team, as well as the game's realistic setting. As well, the actual depiction of these scenarios is fitting to their concept. There is a high risk warrant service against a serial killer, and very rarely does the game give him an accomplice, making for *two* suspects. Suspects' abilities and behaviour will fit the situation and their background. You can expect a frightened drug addict to be inaccurate and easier to subdue than a hardened terrorist.

[h2] What's Good? [/h2] 

For all I have said about the game's flaws, I want to note what the game has done right. RoN is a passion project with the efforts of a committed dev team, and it does show.
 - When the game is not losing frames and stuttering, it can look very good! Even if I would rather trade the picture for a consistent framerate, it is genuinely nice to look at.
 - Teammate AI. This has faced a massive overhaul in the recent update, and for the better. The SWAT teammates are incredibly helpful, approach situations with initiative, and rarely obstruct the player.
 - The game's shooting mechanics are on point, as long as you're not stuttering. The firearm mechanics are well simulated, impacts are well communicated and the different firing positions and optics have real use cases.

Giving a negative review until they fix the busted ass suspect AI — It is seriously egregious, for how central suspects are to the enjoyment of the game. I didn't have a problem with some shoddy AI until they decided to claim this game was 1.0 ready. Going to give a very thoughtful and thorough breakdown of the AI issues.

TL;DR: The suspect AI is extremely shallow, and the devs compensated the difficulty by making them all John Wick level threats. 

[b]The Rules of Engagement Paradox:[/b]
Gun wielders do not surrender unless shot, period. Think about what that does in a game where shooting is supposed to be a last resort. You are punished as it incurs RoE penalties, but no amount of surprise, intimidation, or advantage will convince them not to essentially commit suicide by cop.

This behaviour was clearly such an obstacle for plausible SWAT gameplay that the devs compensated by making nearly everything short of a headshot or dismemberment less-than-lethal. It is truly wild how much lead suspects will endure and still not die.

[b]The 250ms Problem:[/b]
Every suspect has a flat 250ms time (spotting you -> raising weapon -> aiming -> shooting you center mass). This time is flat even if they are facing away from you, surprised, and you are in a pitch black room.

For reference, if you had an equivalent targeting speed in AimLab, you would be 99th percentile in the world. And this is assuming a first person shooter environment where guns have no momentum, not a simulation of real shooting.

My reaction time as a player is about 210ms to *spot* a stimulus and panic-click, which leaves about 40ms to determine if they are armed, if they are intending to surrender, and to aim (non-lethally). This is just genuinely impossible to do consistently, and implies that every gun-wielding maniac in this game has 99th-percentile reaction times and 99th-percentile quick-draw aiming times. (For reference [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hlVp1OIXTqk]here is a clip[/url] I took post 1.0 launch.) 

The only exception is if you are holding shift and exploiting the door-peak mechanic to open doors silently. It seems to break the AI completely and their reaction time and aggression will completely dissolve. I'm talking 15 second delays where you can't tell if the AI is just broken or the game is trying to simulate a standoff (poorly).

[b]The Fix (IMO):[/b]
A much improved suspect AI would take between 150ms-3000ms to spot you (depending on light conditions, distance, sound), and then between 100 and 1200ms to aim depending on if they're already aiming at you, or if their gun is unreadied and they're facing away from you. In my opinion their training should also impact this aim time.

Additionally, (and this is more opinionated) there should be between 50ms and 10 seconds of additional psychological delay which lets you defuse the situation, or at least give you some decision-making time. In reality, being ambushed by a SWAT team would be terrifying (especially when multiple doors are breached simultaneously, with explosives, shotguns, kicks) and most suspects would either dive for cover, flee, try to wrestle control back by bargaining or threatening violence, or just surrender on sight to save their own life.

Only the most unstable and far-gone criminals would (when aimed at by 5 swat officers' rifles) decide the best course of action is to unload on all 5 of them without hesitation. And with those types, I feel like they'd be equally likely to turn their gun on themselves.

So all-in-all this would turn a 250ms flat delay into:
- A minimum of 300ms for a camping, pre-aimed, pre-aggressive gunmen.
- Between 2s and 4.2s for low visibility detection on an unreadied (but aggressive) gunman
- Somewhere typically between 3s and 10s for an untrained, nervous, unreadied, gunman. This delay which can be used to defuse and intimidate the suspect.

If you disagree (this game has a lot of 'skill issue' types), I challenge you to record your own gameplay and watch how long it takes *you* to identify a person, identify their threat level, aim, and fire. 
If it's longer than 250ms on average then I rest my case. If you are consistently faster than 250ms then you're probably playing like a mass shooter and not like a SWAT officer. I'd also guess that you're leaning heavily on map knowledge, spawn knowledge, and predictable AI exploits (silent door peak exploit, pepper spray camping).

[b]Tangent: The problem with the 'skill issue' types[/b] is that they wilfully disregard the difference between fun, realistic difficulty and cheap, time-wasting difficulty. To them, difficulty is self-justifying, and they will talk down to good-faith criticisms that would make their game more fun. I think it's some culture-war bullshit that hasn't left their brain for over a decade, but they will defend simply bad game design like a dog backed into a corner.

My response to that type of player is that *I don't think the game is too difficult*. I just think the game does an incredibly poor job at simulating one of its largest sim elements: the suspects. The game *should* be difficult (probably more difficult than it already is) but that difficulty should come from the decision-making, not reaction times. 

When you breach a room full of gunmen, the difficulty should be found in navigating a complex environment of psychology, choice lethality, choice non-lethality, civilian safety, other objectives (bomb defusal, hostage safety), minimizing officer injury, and keeping order after the guns have stopped firing. That stuff is wayyyy more interesting than shooting.

Currently, there is virtually zero decisionmaking. Every room is incredibly simple — a game of whack-a-mole where (one way or another) everyone in that room has the same dogmatic dedication to killing all law enforcement they can. They will pull not one, not two, but three separate weapons on you, they do not feel fear, and their only priority is killing cops, even above their own life, even above doing the very crime they intended to do in the first place. It just kinda sucks. It's so flat.

[b]The ESP Problem:[/b]
Suspects will track your body through walls with ESP once they begin firing their clip, they will continue to unload their magazine at your body penetrating through doors, walls, objects even if they haven't seen you for a full second. (Here is [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HEWlv_ECKak]a clip[/url] showing this issue.)

This would be less of an issue if they merely fired at the edge of the cover, but no, they track your body even if you are moving and 5 feet inside cover. [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hz33pR9axmU]This clip[/url] shows that they can even shoot you with no reference point.

[b]Lack of Decisionmaking:[/b]
The only way to follow RoE is to either flashbang every room (removes all decisionmaking), or to play the game at a snail's pace while shooting suspects on-sight with pepperballs or beanbags (removes all decisionmaking). Neither of these playstyles are fun, and neither are realistic.

From what I can tell, of the flat 250ms it takes for a suspect to shoot you, 200ms is to spot you, and 50ms is time-to-aim. (Evidenced by [url=https://youtu.be/a5pCZAARwNs?t=19]this clip[/url].) To the player, the raise gun animation will barely have perceptually started by the time they've already clocked you in the shoulder.

[b]Flashlights Need Buff:[/b]
Light discipline *should* affect spotting time, but flashlights should reduce the accuracy and aim-time of gunmen. Currently, because it does not affect aim, it seems to have precisely the opposite effect it should. Flashlights right now only serve to start the 250ms timer the second a door is opened. I refer back to the [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hlVp1OIXTqk]earlier clip[/url].

Ready or Not is a very realistic FPS with many admirable gimmicks that enrich the gameplay and make it very immersive for one to take control of a HRT (Human Rescue Team). It's filled with many objectives and a hard-to-learn gameplay which doesn't allow for many mistakes. 
Having said that, it's still in its infancy (not supprising for an early access game), and I will go on about a few things I'd like the developers to consider to make this game even better:

NPC behavior:
The NPCs take the iniciative very often in the gameplay and take other routes to supprise the players. I'd like to note that they are a bit unrealistic in their reaction times and behavior in a few aspects. For example they instantly understand the ongoing situation and the presence of police (even when not noticed beforehand through flashlights etc.), which doesn't seem quite right for me. It's also nearly impossible to supprise the NPCs unless you face them from the back. It would be helpful if one could sneak around an NPC or supprise them from behind so that a stealthy gameplay is more likely.

I would also address the issue that civilians slowly move away from you, if not shouted at proximitaly. I'd assume that most civilains are quite happy and therefore not as affraid in such a situation to move away from a clearly recognisable police officer trying to help them (a bit like in SWAT 4).

NPC behavior (friendly):
Most of the time your teammates are quite helpfull in clearing a room or space, but there are still a few unaddressed issues I'd like to talk about: 
When clearing a room the position of the NPCs (friendly) is not always accurate. This way it sometimes happens that they stand in the middle of a room during a 'clearing' command, whereas others stand correctly near the doorway. 
Also the AI seems to have an issue with you (as a player) standing slightly in their way (even though there's a way to get by exactly besides you)!
It's also quite hard to complete a mission without unnecessary casualties because the AI likes to shoot (even enemies only carrying a knife) very rapidly and most of the time with unnecessary force (i.e. in the chest or head).

Objective placement:
This issue is very simple: I would find it more realistic and interesting, if objectives/evidence (like a laptop or crystal meth packages) were placed in other locations everytime you play the same mission. This way it's not only running along the same routes and therefore needs more focus to locate the given items. Otherwise it can be very monotonous to play the exact same mission multiple times and already knowing the location from the start.


In the last paragraph I want to make clear that in most aspects I really like the game and it's gameplay, though sometimes unrealistic, it is quite immersive and challenging to master a mission with good grades! 
I really hope the developers take this into account when dealing with these issues and make the game even more realistic than before. More maps are also welcomed but I'm sure they are already working on that regard!
Otherwise I highly recommend for you to check out the game yourself and form your own opinion of it!

This game is the tactical shooter I have been waiting for. It's a slow (no sprint), methodical, and tense experience unlike any other game I've played, broken up by intense and unforgiving shootouts. There are 18 maps currently and the random placement of enemies and civilians make each game a different experience. The Police aspect adds gameplay aspects that are new to me: The idea of "Rules of Engagement" and non-lethal takedowns are a great style but totally avoidable if you don't care about score. Which I try not to.

The game is obviously meant to be played with friends but the single player experience is pretty good in it's own way. You only get AI squad mates when playing solo but being able to order them around changes the strategy nicely. It does mean that playing solo with 4 bots can be easier than playing with only 2 players. I haven't tried to play with other public players.

The npc activities are incredibly well done. Enemies will play dead or fake a surrender, and take civilians as human shields. civilians will panic and flee if there's too much going on. An npc you thought was safe could pick up a fallen gun while you look away and turn on you.

I really like the slow progression of difficulty between each levels, almost every level adds in a new mechanic that you have to look out for like trip mines, new enemy behaviour, and threats (although it does mean that early levels could become boring for lacking these mechanics).

There are no equipment unlocks, meaning that you start with all the tools and can try out everything to find a setup that works. Which might change depending on the mission select. Some customisation options are locked behind level score requirements but most are pretty easy to get.

When all the objectives of a mission are completed the game ends and you are given a score depending on how you did. This score is strictly for achievements/bragging rights and don't negatively impact you. It's based mostly heavly on 1: Completing level objectives 2: Rescuing all the civilians and 3: Keeping the players alive. You get bonus points for taking the "Suspects" (the bad guys) alive but it isn't required to complete the level. Some levels have objectives for taking specific Suspects alive but the mission doesn't fail if you kill them. I've "completed" levels with an F rank before and probably will again.

The game is DIFFICULT. The enemies are merciless and great at holding angles, flanking, and taking you by surprise. As of right now, there is a lot of talk about the bots being TOO strong: reacting too fast and being too accurate. My opinion is that they're mostly fine. I've seen very few instances of them being aimbot/wall hacking. The fast reaction can be worked around by moving slowly and avoiding doors that they're actively guarding will allow you to get the jump on them. When the bullets start flying though it's better to get behind cover rather than try and out shoot them.

One downside that all of my friends ran into was the Tutorial being broken in some way or another. It's a bad first introduction to the game.

If you're looking for a slower more tactical shooter then you might love this game, there's already a lot of content to enjoy and I'm looking forward to additional content that is likely to come at some point in the future. Also there's already a large modding community releasing content but I haven't tried any mods yet.

To cut to the chase: is Ready of Not better or worse than SWAT 4?

My answer: worse, but by a hair's breadth.

The game definitely doesn't hide that it's a spiritual sequel to the 2005 tactical first person shooter, so that's the framing i'm going to work with.

The Good:

From a mechanical point of view, everything here seems to work as good or better than SWAT 4. If you know that game, you'll instantly understand what you're playing. If you want a game about tactical room clearing, QCB, hostage rescue and police proceedure, this is your game.

From an presentation point of view, at least on paper, it understood the homework SWAT 4 set. The levels are very much the star of the one-act play you turned up late to. Just like SWAT 4, (and to a degree, Thief, of whuch we don't talk enough about how much DNA there was in SWAT 4), you are interloping in a story that has already played out- and it has the same suitably eerie feel to it.

This is a dark, noir, dytopian (alternate-version? questionable!) of California, and you are its depressed, violent garbagemen.

The Bad:

What takes RoN down from a ten to probably an eight is the lack of character.

Your fellow officers are randomly generated faces with whom you build no raport. Even though they're not completely lacking in personality, they lack the little quirks that the unit from SWAT 4 did, and that really detracts from the game. It doesn't feel like just another day on the job in the same way. Fixed recurring characters like your superiors and fellow SWAT subordiantes would have made marked difference.

I think also a lack of progression hurts the feeling of strategy as you complete missions. You will fairly quickly find a balanced configuration that suits how you like to get things done.

In SWAT 4 you are similarly given all the toys to play with from the start, however, SWAT 4 was made in a time when SWAT and counter-terrorism were going through radical change. Back then, there was still a bit more of a dichotamy between different weapons that had different strengths and weaknesses, and body-armor wasn't quite as common.

Contemporary operators typically tend to use some kind of short-barreled rifle in most situations. I feel there should have been some kind of progression system to unlock things gradually, so that you have to use some of the more archaic weapons first and build up to the more ubiquitous ones. Either that, or there should have been fewer weapons with more of a trade-off between them.

I think the intention here is to make your loadout choices fairly grandualar and based on preference/feel rather than there being a power curve or some kind of rock-paper-scissors trinity of different weapon choices. To a degree though, it also makes your choices about how to outfit your team feel a bit pointless beyond "do you want to equip the cool retro MP5 or do you want to give them something that will actually take down a perp before they unload a whole magazine into you".

This stuff about weapons though, is sort of a nitpick, I don't count it strongly against the game. I like playing dress up with my police operator dolls.

The Ugly:

The bit that actually does harm the game is all the controversy baiting stuff. Some of the levels are very clearly referencing specific real world incidents and places, some of them are SWAT 4 levels but with the themes and deco turned up to 11.

The game has some levels that seem more or less engineered to "shocking". I don't care about it being too topical or bad taste or brutally honest or whatever. I care more about the execution, and I think they could have actually made it more gripping or chilling or emotionally impactful by just toning it down a bit.

The phrase "I know some writers that use subtlety and they're all cowards" definitely springs to mind. You'll encounter multiple "crazy writing on the walls rooms" throughout the game, sometimes once per level. It starts to wear a bit thin after a while. It isn't authentic or mature or "showing the dark underbelly of America that we tolerate within our homes and workplaces", it's just a bit hackneyed after a while.

Some of the levels I enjoyed the most were actually ones that were a bit more mundane- a gas station, a use car lot, an office. The sort of domesticity of these locations without crazy writing walls or mountains of bodies or lots of drawings that looked like they've been ripped directly from Artstation, made it feel so much more grounded and believable.

When something is trying its hardest to be eyes-wide-shut, in the service of showing that something terrible and topical is happening in real life, it really doesn't sell that message if it's all the time.

If someone ever makes a level that asks the player to suspend thier disbelief at the idea that people spent hours decorating the creepy pedophile room- it comes off as sophomoric rather than mature. Little St James island has a bunch of weird creepy shit on it, but Jeffrey Epstien didn't scrawl "I love kids" all over the walls. It's the understatedness that makes you introspect on how sordid it feels.

8.5/10.

I bought this game like 2 days ago, and have already racked up over 22 hours of playtime. During my sleep I dream of clearing rooms, and wake up in a cold sweat when I see a black woman with a tec 9. 11/10. Please hire me SWAT.

Actual SWAT operator here for a pretty large city. I have to say, this is the first law enforcement game I've ever played where I don't have any big gripes with the gameplay or premise. Right down to the tiny details like the tactical acronyms written on the whiteboards at the station, you can tell that real-life tactical guys were heavily involved with how it was made. They did a fantastic job making something that is a really fun game and an excellent buddy shooter while still trying very hard to keep it realistic. It isn't perfect, but here I am playing a videogame about my job and enjoying it so they definitely are doing something right.

It's also really cool to see a game that takes the tactical side of policework and the unique dilemmas we face and puts them front and center for people to mess around with and think about, and for that, I am very grateful to the developers. Most of what we do stays pretty well out of the public eye and I think this kind of exposure is great. Maybe this will lead to some budget increases and I can finally get a third pair of BDUs!

Okay so let me start by saying that this game is not for everyone. If you expect a fast-paced shooter like Rainbow Six Siege then this game is the opposite of what you are likely looking for.

For people that enjoy intense tactical gameplay and slow-paced thought-through approaches this is one of the only games that comes close to what the SWAT series offered.

No sprint! (You can lower your weapon to move a bit faster but you can't just Leroy around)

Man I love that. Not being able to sprint makes the game so much more smooth to play in random groups. Everything takes a bit of time and you can think how you stack up and breach. 

Noone can really go Rambo and the ones that try it are send back to the spectator screen within seconds.

Gadgets are currently limited in choice but present the foundation of what you need. 

You got Gas and Flash Grenades as well as another LTL-Grenade named "Stinger". 

Breaching can be done by means of Explosives. Battering Rams, Breaching shotguns or just old-school kicking the doors down. You can also use door wedges to block off escape routes or entry points.

Equipment wise there are NVG, ballistic vests and helmets as well as gas masks and flash resistant masks.

Weapon selection isn't half bad with a few Assault Rifles, Shotguns and MP's to choose from with different sidearms to go with them. You also have LTL options like a pepper ball gun, bean bag shotgun and a taser as pistol gadget.

Map design is different and challenging while some are more detailed than others you can already see quite some attention to detail in the "first" level while others still lack a bit of "life" which the Dev's already commented on is getting added but they wanted some levels ready to be played with.

Each level comes with different scenarios, you need to follow general RoE and it's really tense trying to get everyone (including the gunman) out alive.

The game also adds some information that makes you want to take the shooters into custody like telling you that the shooters at the gas station are juvenile and the robbery went wrong.

It really hits the spot with tight and incredibly short firefights that are over within a couple seconds where 90% of the mission is spend going around, using every tool you have to avoid direct confrontation and you get rewarded for it accordingly. 

For it being an EA title I can only recommend this game for people that are looking for a slow tactical shooter like SWAT 4.

 (Which is really cheap to grab right now for only around 5€, just keep in mind that SWAT 4 is from 2005 and looks and plays accordingly. But it gives you a really good indication of what RoN will feel like, although RoN is much more unforgiving in reaction times. So if you are unsure if you want to invest into this game then go ahead and try this first.)

The game of course needs some more work to be done in terms of AI behaviour and some more levels / scenarios but if this is the first playable build in EA and we see regular updates after the holidays this game could become a true marvel of it's genre.

Ready or Not isn't a bad game. It's simply not the game it claims or wants to be. Originally intended as a spiritual successor to SWAT 4 (which you can find on GoG for cheap, I highly recommend it), RoN boasts sleek and modern graphics, on a modern engine with solid gunplay and a host of new features. While I really do enjoy it, it is simply flawed and frustrating and here's a couple of the core reasons why;

Gameplay:

Ready or Not's gunplay is one of its key features, you have a wide array of weaponry to choose from, (mostly) limited to the varieties which various armed police response forces use. Beyond cyclic rate, magazine capacity and which calibre and ammunition type is used, your weapon choice isn't all that important, because ultimately they all shoot more than straight enough to hit what you aim at. This is all fine, if only it weren't for the AI of the people you might have to use these tools against.

Suspect AI is not very good, and tends to begin manoeuvering like a prime boxer and magdumping the player with inhuman accuracy once they realise you're there. Suspects and bystanders alike don't often give up, as if it's roll of the dice rather than a reaction to immediate threats and the internal psychology of the individual. Whether civilian, junkie, petty criminal or heavily armed terrorist, the experience of trying to take them into custody is universal. Less than lethal means to resolve these situations are available, but in practice feel like only a mild suggestion for the target to comply rather than a forceful impetus. A gang member can take multiple beanbag shots, and after letting him perform his little animation of agony each time, he just reverts back to his state of utter defiance. In many cases will still raise his weapon and force you to make the decision to either roll the dice again in the hopes he will give up or draw a weapon with a bit more bodily harm involved. That is to say, they're not very useful.

Friendly AI is often critiqued here, but I personally don't have too much that jumps to mind which I might complain about besides how unclear what counts as a room can be (and thus makes how far your team goes something of guesswork), and the fact that you can't issue orders to them through your helmet cam as you can in SWAT 4, which can really slow the pace of a lightning raid as you slooowly go from A to B to co-ordinate, say, an approach to the roof of the Brixley talent agency from two directions at once. 

This shooting gallery approach is also reflected in the scoring, where an itchy trigger finger isn't at all punished, so long as you yell "police" beforehand and the target isn't a prime suspect. Otherwise, you're free to ventilate The Poors with impunity. Comparing this to its inspiration, SWAT 4 where even just a few dead suspects might cost you the level, placing a lot of consequence on that decision to pull the trigger, reveals that Ready or Not is more a shooter than a simulator. For a game that tries to depict the responsiblity of police in spite of what their morals and mental state might say, its core gameplay loop is inherently at odds with this intent.

Story and Worldbuilding:

This isn't something that most people would care about, but when a game is touted as a successor to the SWAT games, it's one of the things that some people will pay attention to. Atmosphere and environmental storytelling are quite well done in Ready or Not as a whole, presenting to the player a fictional Los Angeles on the verge of descent into anarchy and chaos. Levels are littered with items and details that successfully sell the illusion of this universal decline and the lives affected by it, ordinary or not. Quite a few of these little details are not so much clues as they are confessions, and the set dressing places them everywhere to the point that you don't need to even pay attention to the level to understand what's really going on behind the scenes.

The key moments that complete this image of a grim reality are flawed to say the least, relying upon scale and shock to hammer it home. These moments were memorable, if absurd at times, and many people who played it will attest to this - at least until the 1.0 update stripped these moments of the details which made them so. Scale and lack of subtlty are what holds RoN back because it starts to become cliche and unbelievable. This is no longer environmental storytelling, it's just a poorly implemented diegetic TL;DR of the entire level. Ultimately it's ambitious, but clumsy, exaggerated and inconsistent, giving us horrible crimes but without the grounding or tact to convincingly sell them to the audience.

Mods:

Ultimately the worst injustice in my opinion is the constant breaking of mods. For a game that has only limited levels and weapons, even with DLC included, community content greatly increases the enjoyment and longievity of the game. There was a great number of great mods when I began playing, but with every major update, most of them are broken and only a few creators bother to update them given how tedious the process is. Apparently this is a result of Unreal Engine 5, but it's still criminal to me and is no doubt a bar to entry for many who might like to make a mod. Of course, your effort might be wasted simply because of an inevitable update. Sadly I will never again get to clear a Boeing 747 full of hijackers, with no equipment but a TLE1911, flashbangs, and one buddy who brought a .357 Magnum, and nor will you unless you happen to have it all backed up and know your way around the Unreal modding process. That experience was one of the highs of this game for me, and what kept me coming back to it, but now it's lost to time and so is the key reason I would re-install.

There are many things I probably forgot to include in this review but I don't want to write a whole essay. I'll update it as more things come to mind. I would recommend Ready or Not, but ONLY if you can get it on sale and are willing to put up with the AI ruining the experience. Until at least that changes though, and I do really hope it changes, it will remain a middling 6/10 in my books.

After sinking nearly 300 hours into Ready or Not as a veteran player and pledger throughout the games alpha stages, after S-ranking every Base and DLC mission, unlocking every achievement, and combing through the games lore, I can confidently say that VOiD Interactive has created a wonderfully immersive and unique, tactical narrative experience that I unfortunately cannot recommend that you purchase at full price in its current state.

At its core, Ready or Not is probably one of the best tactical shooters to grace the genre. Every map in this game, even the "bad ones" that I'd rather not play through more than a couple of times, have very thoughtfully crafted atmospheres that you simply cannot find anywhere else. The gunplay is thrilling, the core mechanics and suspect interaction systems are well executed, and the wide variety of tactical equipment and weaponry that the game gives you allow you to play the way you want while maintaining a slow, deliberate pace that rewards careful planning over just rushing into engagements.

All of that being said though, the game is far from perfect. There is a lot of undisclosed AI generated content that frankly, I find to be quite egregious in certain areas of the game. VOiD has shown themselves to be perfectly capable as writers, modelers, animators, and map designers through the years but taking even a quick glance at things like posters or artwork within the environment, mission debriefs, and even the mission select screen show that the developers are perfectly fine with cutting corners for no real reason other than pure laziness; though this can be explained away as "Le small indie developer needs to spend these resources elsewhere."

My biggest issue with the game, however, comes down to the Suspect and officer AI. It is incredibly hard to ignore once you've spent even a small amount of time playing the game. Even on standard difficulties the suspect AI has for years felt wildly overtuned with suspects reacting near instantly to the slightest of sounds, seemingly having 360 degree fields of vision, most times spotting you through solid objects in areas that should have very limited visibility, and have a hard coded 70% chance to just headshot and instakill you with even the smallest of calibers whether they be a trained combat veteran or a lowly gas station robber. On top of this, their behaviors are incredibly inconsistent. One second they can be hostile, and the next they're completely passive making encounters with them feel like a complete RNG fest rather than something you can learn from. 

On the other hand, your own officer AI can find themselves struggling to path correctly and often rigidly block doorways like their names are Lydia and Faendal. They occasionally ignore your commands, get stuck on geometry, or fail to dynamically react to pretty much anything correctly. They make everything feel uncoordinated and come off as tools that require immense micromanagement rather than a part of your team.  The civilians add yet another layer of frustration to this, again, with inconsistent and unrealistic behaviors. Why are they behaving with such defiant hostility to you and your team when they should be behaving like the frightened hostages they're described to be in mission briefings? 

The incredibly strict achievements that the game has also compound these issues, many of them were for the longest time unable to be unlocked because they were either bugged or were unnecessarily frustrating to obtain because of their undisclosed requirements. The game being hard isn't something I'm faulting it for, I prefer it that way actually. My issue is that the difficulty feels artificially inflated and unfair, which makes the experience feel unrewarding and, at times, even disrespectful of the player’s time. What makes it more disappointing is that these issues are so consistent that they have been consistently voiced by the playerbase and it’s hard not to question how much of the game is being thoroughly playtested.

These issues in an otherwise standout title don't quite ruin the game for me, but it does heavily chip away at the experience that VOiD is trying to sell to you, and that's why you should be cautious when buying this game.
